OptionWorld: A Benchmark for Diagnosing Failures of LLMs
as Long-Term Personal Assistants

Ruoyu Zhang1 Zhaocen Liu1 Weiyi Tian2 zhangruoy@outlook.com liu0411@student.ubc.ca weiyitian@uchicago.edu
Melissa Feng3 Shilong Liu4,∗ mxf4246@nyu.edu shilong.liu@princeton.edu
1University of British Columbia  2University of Chicago
3Independent Researcher  4Princeton University  ∗Corresponding author
Abstract

Long-term assistants must follow unfinished tasks across days as information and circumstances change. Finding information or starting an action, however, does not ensure that the task gets completed. We introduce OptionWorld, a benchmark that traces information acquisition, judgments, actions, and outcomes in simulated daily-life tasks to identify where current LLMs fall short as long-term personal assistants. In runs with archived decision inputs, the key facts remain in the model’s last input before the deadline in 35.5% of failed instances. Failure analysis identifies the three most frequent problems: needed information is not obtained or combined, available opportunities to act go unused, and agents impose restrictions that the task does not require. Three follow-up experiments show that supplying missing facts restores task success in some cases; action reminders can restart work while subsequent steps still miss the deadline; and correcting a supplied note that wrongly forbids contact restores permitted inquiry. These findings locate shortcomings in maintaining task state: connecting facts to unfinished work, following through before deadlines, and separating actual restrictions from the agent’s assumptions.

1 Introduction

The problem: sustaining follow-through. LLM agents use language models to choose actions through tools, such as reading records or contacting people (Yao et al., 2023). Agents also retain memories and reflections (Packer et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023). As long-term personal assistants, they must follow unfinished work as information, deadlines, and user needs change. For example, an insurer may report an unpaid premium despite an earlier bank receipt (Figure 1). The assistant must connect the records, follow updated permission to consult both parties, and complete the user-approved action before the deadline. Maintaining task state means tracking unfinished work, permitted next steps, and their deadlines. We ask where current LLMs fall short in this responsibility and what support helps them resume progress.

Our approach: locating where tasks stall. Existing benchmarks examine task execution, memory, and proactive assistance (Zhou et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Pasternak et al., 2025; Studio and AI, 2026). Task and stage scores alone, however, leave open whether a failed target lacked necessary facts, retained those facts without using them effectively, or stalled during subsequent action. Distinguishing these problems requires connecting outcomes to the information and decisions behind them. We introduce OptionWorld, a benchmark of simulated insurance, work, housing, and other ongoing matters. Agents discover needs through daily events and records without seeing the evaluation targets. For each target, we connect fact acquisition, the facts still visible at decision time, judgments, actions, and outcomes across days to locate where progress stops.

Main findings: information is only part of the problem. The three most frequent problems concern connecting facts to unfinished work and updating next steps: missing or unassembled information, unused follow-ups or retries, and restrictions the agent adds without a basis in the task. The fact-acquisition analysis finds that nearly half of failures occur after the primary facts were obtained in time. In runs with archived inputs, over one-third of failures still have those facts in the last valid decision input. Failure therefore extends beyond information acquisition. Cross-day records help explain how obstacles develop: one agent saves a rejection as a requirement to wait for another record and continues waiting days later, although the rejection never imposed that condition. Here, memory preserves a mistaken interpretation that guides later inaction.

Exploratory follow-ups test whether targeted support restores progress: adding missing facts recovers some tasks, while reminders can restart an action without completing the remaining work in time. A controlled permission-note experiment further shows that correcting a supplied false contact ban restores permitted inquiry while actual no-contact rules remain respected.

The main contributions of this work:

  • •

    A benchmark testing whether assistants discover needs and complete tasks across days under changing information and permissions.

  • •

    A target-level analysis exposing unused follow-ups and unsupported restrictions preserved in memory despite available key facts.

  • •

    Three support experiments distinguishing recovery of a permitted action from completion of the original task.

2 Related Work

Agent methods and benchmarks.

Generative Agents uses memory-based planning (Park et al., 2023), MemGPT manages memory tiers (Packer et al., 2023), and Voyager accumulates reusable skills (Wang et al., 2024). To evaluate agents, task-execution benchmarks ask whether they can complete a request (Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024). Memory benchmarks ask whether agents can recall and update information from earlier interactions (Wu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026). Proactive-assistance benchmarks ask when to offer help and how to uncover users’ unstated needs or preferences (Liu et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026), while other benchmarks test whether agents notice later changes or remember to act when needed (Shi et al., 2026; Liu and Gabriel, 2026). These abilities support discovering and following up on users’ needs (Table 1, left). We study how agents combine them across days: why do they stop following up or miss deadlines as information changes?

Locating failures and testing support.

AgentBoard measures intermediate progress to analyze agent behavior beyond final success (Ma et al., 2024). PROBE separately scores finding documents, identifying the problem, and specifying an action (Pasternak et al., 2025). VibeLifeBench checks behavior and task state across multiple weeks (Studio and AI, 2026). Claw-Anything tests how access to events and the amount of context affect performance (Lin et al., 2026). Repeated-success measures check whether agents complete the same tasks consistently across runs (Yao et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2026). OptionWorld links these questions: which targets repeatedly fail, and where does progress stop within them? We connect source access and problem recognition to each target’s key facts at decision time, subsequent actions, and outcome feedback (Table 1, right).

3 Benchmark and Evaluation Design

3.1 Worlds and Interaction

OptionWorld contains eight authored daily-life simulations spanning housing, work, independent living, and family coordination. A target is a specific issue to discover and address. Each 60-day world contains 24 targets, totaling 192. Agents receive broad responsibilities, so they must discover these needs from events and records without seeing the target list. Evaluator-only specifications define required evidence, response periods, and success conditions. Tasks may require comparing records across sources or days, noticing that expected events have not occurred, or seeking clarification or authorization.

Daily inputs contain events, lists of available records, saved notes, registered monitoring conditions, and feedback. Tools let the agent inspect and compare records, save notes, contact relevant parties, request approval, and carry out authorized operations. Visible rules specify what is allowed and whose approval is required. Delayed replies may resolve only part of an issue, requiring further updates and follow-up (Figure 1).

3.2 Evidence-to-Outcome Criteria

To locate where progress stops, we score the outcome and the preceding evidence, judgments, and actions. Success requires feedback confirming that the agent preserved a choice the user would otherwise lose or resolved the issue. For example, confirmed protection of a pending clinic pickup preserves an option; an accepted inquiry alone does not establish that outcome.

Each target receives six binary scores per run: Observed (OO). The agent accessed a designated relevant source or record; this does not necessarily provide all required facts. For example, a source listing does not show the contents of each record. Risk hypothesis (HH). It identified the specific problem or risk associated with the target. Grounded discovery (GG). Its judgment was supported by the required evidence already obtained in the interaction. Timely grounded discovery (TT). Its supported judgment fell within the target’s response period. Intervention delivered (II). A target-specific external action received an acceptance receipt and met the requirements for evidence, timing, and permission specified for that target. Simulated outcome (YY). Feedback linked to that action and target confirmed that the user’s option was preserved or the issue resolved.

Scores report confirmed credit. Unresolved review judgments retain a separate uncertainty flag, reported as unknown in the follow-ups. Our main score, the option-preservation rate (OPR), is the success fraction: OPR=K−1​∑r=1KYr\mathrm{OPR}=K^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{K}Y_{r}. Each target in each run counts as one instance; KK is their total number.

Separating source access (OO) from problem recognition (HH), and accepted intervention (II) from outcome (YY), locates different breaks in progress. Scores satisfy H≥G≥T≥I≥YH\geq G\geq T\geq I\geq Y: later criteria require the earlier ones. These dependencies govern scoring, not action order.

3.3 Evaluation Protocol

We evaluate DeepSeek, Fable, Gemini, Grok, Qwen, and Astra (Codex) on the same eight worlds, with three runs per world: 144 trajectories and 3,456 target instances in total. Five systems use the same runner, which starts a new conversation each day while carrying forward saved notes, monitoring conditions, and feedback; previously accessed records remain retrievable. Astra uses a separate local Codex execution setup. In runs with archived inputs, we check whether each failed target’s primary facts remain in its last decision input within the allowed action period, distinguishing earlier acquisition from availability at decision time.

All trajectories use the same scoring rules. Two LLM reviewers independently inspect records with the evaluated system’s identity hidden. Their judgments are combined with checks of action timing, acceptance receipts, and outcome feedback. Multiple human reviewers also examined all 144 trajectories. Appendices B–D give world construction, execution settings, prompts, and scoring examples.

4 Main Results and Failure Analysis

4.1 Task Completion & Where Progress Stops

Under the specified environment budgets, Table 2 reports target success from 23.6% to 61.6%: even the highest-scoring system leaves more than one-third unfinished. Astra has the highest success rate (61.6%), followed by DeepSeek (48.3%).

Broader source access does not ensure more completed tasks.

Astra has lower source-access coverage than DeepSeek (85.1% versus 96.5%) and has similar timely grounded discovery (77.8% versus 78.1%), yet delivers more interventions (68.6% versus 57.1%) and completes more targets. Source access records whether at least one relevant source was accessed, rather than the amount of information gathered. To compare follow-through on the same tasks, we match 275 instances for which both systems make timely grounded judgments and have no uncertain stage labels. Astra delivers 268 interventions and completes 262 targets; DeepSeek delivers 227 and completes 207.

In a paired trajectory, both systems identify conflicting weekly availability requirements. Astra obtains authorization and submits a protective correction request, leaving the factual reconciliation to the responsible record holder; DeepSeek saves the discrepancy and waits for that holder to become available. Recognized uncertainty can thus lead either to a permitted protective step or to continued monitoring (Appendix J.3).

Recognizing a problem can still leave the next step undone.

Grok makes timely grounded judgments for 50.2% of targets but delivers interventions for only 28.0%, ending with the lowest success rate (23.6%). Of its 289 timely judgments, 128 do not lead to a qualifying intervention. The bottleneck differs from Gemini’s earlier gap: Gemini accesses sources for 87.5% of targets but identifies a specific risk for only 56.2%. Even among 239 matched instances with timely primary facts and no uncertain stage judgments for either DeepSeek or Grok, they deliver 185 and 127 interventions, respectively. In a supplier-payment case, both obtain a credit memo and a conflicting full-debit record. Grok records the conflict and a watchpoint; DeepSeek obtains confirmation and executes the approved action before the deadline (Appendices J and J.4).

Could these gaps instead reflect missing or forgotten facts? Across all six systems and three runs, 1,038 of 2,096 failures (49.5%) occur after the agent obtains all designated primary facts before the deadline (Figure 2b). For the five systems sharing a runner, the input-visibility analysis uses only Runs 2–3, where decision inputs are archived: 460 of their 1,295 failures (35.5%) still contain those facts in the last input within the allowed action period (Appendix I, Table 20).

Similar scores conceal different successes and activity.

Fable and Qwen complete 208 and 206 of 576 instances, respectively, but these are not the same successful tasks. They disagree on 150 matched outcomes: 76 favor Fable and 74 favor Qwen. The difference remains on 78 of 249 matched instances where both obtain the primary facts in time and neither has uncertain stage labels. The contrast runs in both directions within the same caregiver world and run, where both systems complete 12 of 24 targets. Fable follows up an unanswered authorization request and completes a care-allowance task; Qwen’s attempts stall after rejected requests. On a childcare funding discrepancy, Qwen follows a partial reply through to clarification and action, while Fable waits for another record before asking. The shared facts still allow different choices: inquire, repair a rejected request, or wait (Appendix J.4).

Nor does Qwen’s greater activity produce a higher total: it makes 12,553 tool calls versus Fable’s 8,049 across the same 24 world–run pairs. Of the 4,504 additional calls, 1,967 (43.7%) are risk reports or watchpoint registrations. Extra activity can thus record and monitor pending matters without acting to resolve them (Appendix K).

Fewer records need not mean easier completion.

Among shared-runner instances with timely grounded judgments and no uncertain stage labels, targets involving an expected event that has not occurred (missing-event) succeed in 90.7% of cases, compared with 68.4% for constraints stated in one record (single-source) and 60.2% for tasks requiring facts from different days (cross-day accumulation). All instances in this comparison have timely primary facts, so the difference remains after discovery. Missing-event tasks proceed through a request to the responsible institution, whereas cross-day tasks require confirmation followed by execution. A task understood from one record is therefore not necessarily easier to complete than one requiring several records: the subsequent action requirements also matter (Appendix J.2).

Repeated runs reveal persistent failures and unstable success.

Do repeated runs overcome the same obstacles? Across all six systems, 64.8% of failed instances come from targets that the same system fails in all three runs (Figure 2a). In the shared-runner group, of 425 model–target pairs failing all three runs, 305 concern targets another system completes at least once. Only 24 of 192 targets fail across all 15 attempts. Persistent failure within one system therefore need not be shared by the others.

Among 301 model–target pairs in this group with timely primary facts, timely grounded judgment, and no uncertain stage labels in any of the three runs, 119 succeed only once or twice and 39 never succeed. Stable discovery does not ensure stable completion. For example, DeepSeek identifies the same pension-record conflict in all three runs. In two it takes a reversible step to preserve the recorded service history; in the third it waits for another record and never delivers an intervention. The repeated difficulty lies in choosing and carrying out an available next step after discovery (Appendices H and J.4). We next trace these failures.

4.2 Failure Profiles and Trajectory Evidence

The three most frequent problems are missing or unassembled information (30.2%), failure to take or adjust an available action (21.3%), and self-imposed restrictions (18.9%). Across all six systems, 2,096 instances are unsuccessful. We exclude 160 involving normal constraints alone, such as quota or permission limits, and classify the remaining 1,936 instances (Table 3). Each receives one label; insufficient evidence (21.3%) is a separate status for instances where the record does not establish a specific problem. Human reviewers checked every LLM-proposed classification against the original trajectory and resolved disagreements before finalizing the labels (Appendix J.1).

Among Fable’s and Qwen’s classified instances, information gaps account for 46.3% and 24.9%, while self-restriction accounts for 23.4% and 29.8%. Their similar overall scores thus accompany different failure profiles: Fable more often lacks needed information, while Qwen more often imposes unsupported restrictions. Grok’s most frequent problem is action selection or adjustment (47.7% of its classified failures), consistent with its large gap between timely judgment and intervention. This category includes choosing an ineffective action or failing to adapt one, not only inaction.

Needed information is not obtained or assembled in time.

The largest category includes facts never retrieved and facts read but not combined or retained for later decisions. Missing facts can remain accessible through record comparison after direct-inspection allowances are exhausted. In a stratified review of 80 shared-runner failures, 35 lack primary facts at the deadline. Replaying comparison tools at saved states confirms this alternative for 15 cases across four systems. Five of these trajectories had already retrieved new facts by comparison elsewhere. Those five expose a strategy-reuse gap: an available, previously used retrieval method is not applied to the unresolved matter after inspection quotas run out (Appendix J.2).

Available actions do not always become effective interventions.

The second category concerns missed follow-ups, retries, or alternative approaches when a permitted opportunity exists. In a Gemini food-business trajectory, the agent notices overlapping inspection and pickup times and tries to ask for clarification on Day 10, when the contact is unavailable. By Day 15, the relevant parties are available; the input still contains both time windows and the user’s preference to keep both options open. Asking for clarification is allowed, with time left before the Day-22 deadline, but the agent does not return to the consultation. Task memory must support reconsidering what to do when a temporary obstacle disappears, not merely preserving the unfinished task (Appendix L).

A contrasting success pattern appears when feedback specifies how to revise a request. When a request is returned for correction or only partly resolved, the feedback names the field to correct and the required source format. We examine instances where both the feedback and its specified follow-up day fall within the deadline. In the shared-runner group, all 99 eligible returned-material instances and all 126 partial-resolution instances receive accepted follow-up requests before the deadline; 91 and 109, respectively, reach the target outcome. For example, Grok rereads a licensing record, supplies the missing case reference with its source, and obtains a resolution. These interactions demonstrate local repair under explicit guidance. Sustained follow-through also requires recognizing when to resume a pending task without such a specific revision instruction, as the missed consultation above illustrates (Appendix J.4).

The agent adds conditions that the task does not require.

Self-restriction turns an unsupported assumption into a reason to wait or stop. In one Qwen trajectory, a rent-review request on Day 19 is rejected with a message that the evidence does not match the specified procedure. Qwen conjectures that another record is missing and saves the instruction “retry after a companion entry.” On Day 24, it explicitly reports not retrying because no such entry has arrived. The rejection never required that record (Appendix D.3).

The same trajectory correctly waits for a daily quota to reset on another matter and retries the next day. It can retry, but does not consistently distinguish environmental requirements from its own explanations: memory can perpetuate mistakes as well as preserve facts. Permission errors similarly remove an allowed next step when a ban on commitment is treated as a ban on inquiry.

Completing a procedure is not the same as resolving the task.

In the shared-runner group, preference, authorization, and multi-party tasks account for 18.2% of target instances but 60.6% of cases with a qualifying intervention and no successful outcome; no such cases occur among single-source, cross-source, or cross-day targets in these runs (Appendix Table 24).

Among 122 multi-party instances with timely facts and judgment and no uncertain stage labels, both consultations, authorized execution, and tool acceptance occur by the deadline, yet 28 fail to meet the target outcome. In a matched DeepSeek mortgage case, both runs consult the parties and execute an approved action. A hardship letter pauses an instalment, but the bank still schedules its full debit. The successful run asks the responsible office to apply a hardship pause; the failed run proposes treating the hardship letter as authoritative and pausing the debit itself. The critical difference is whether the action asks the appropriate party to reconcile the conflict or assumes that the conflict is already settled.

Task state must track both unfinished and completed work.

Less frequent problems are state or updating errors (6.4%) and execution errors (2.0%). A scan of shared-runner trajectories shows that state maintenance also requires stopping completed operations: 69 target instances in 33 trajectories incur 106 repeated-operation rejections after an accepted completion. Forty of these targets are successful under the rubric, so success rates alone miss this redundant activity. The pattern is concentrated in Gemini (59 instances): one trajectory executes on Day 6, receives completion feedback on Day 7, then reuses the same authorization on Days 7, 9, and 13. Together with the missed-retry case, this reveals two directions of state error: leaving a temporary block in place and failing to retire a completed step. Execution errors instead concern parameters, object bindings, or operation order that block an action.

5 Targeted Support for Stalled Tasks

At selected checkpoints, we test three forms of support corresponding to the problems identified in Section 4.2: supplying missing facts, prompting the next permitted action, and clarifying permission boundaries. The first two experiments resume natural failures; the third tests permitted inquiry under externally supplied incorrect permission notes and their corrections.

In the first two experiments, each condition resumes the saved world and agent state (checkpoint) in three continuations through Day 60 with the original model, permissions, budgets, and deadlines. We score new timely intervention (II) and target outcome (YY) under the main-study rules, retaining uncertain scores. Figure 3 summarizes all three experiments; Appendix L gives the continuation protocol and full counts.

5.1 Information: Supplying Missing Evidence

Three Gemini checkpoints cover a contractor’s buyout and a worker’s training hours, the latter from original Runs 2 and 3. The buyout values one campaign, but a ledger lists three renewals, requiring reconciliation by the responsible record holder. The college grants 400 training hours, while certification rules recognize 720 with supervisor proof. In both cases, an allowed comparison can retrieve the missing facts. We compare unchanged continuation (original) with added facts: one researcher-selected comparison-tool call supplies its returned facts and a table of both records. Reformatted facts transposes the same table without changing its contents. Neither supplies an interpretation or action plan.

Added facts restore success at two checkpoints.

At the buyout and Run-3 training checkpoints, added facts raise target success from 0/3 to 3/3 (Figure 3a). Reformatting yields 2/3 successes at each. At Run-2 training, the two support conditions together yield one failure and five uncertain outcomes across six continuations. The uncertain outcomes concern whether the request seeks reconciliation of 400 versus 720 hours or assumes eligibility without supervisory proof.

5.2 Action: Reviewing the Next Step

For inspection–pickup scheduling (Gemini) and shared-car–clinic coordination (DeepSeek), we compare two one-time reminders to review unfinished work under existing permissions. Unlike general review, action review explicitly names follow-up, retry after a lifted restriction, and another permitted approach. Neither adds facts, resources, or a target-specific plan.

Restarting action and finishing in time are different requirements.

Compared with general review, which yields 0/3 qualifying interventions in each case, action review yields 1/3 (Figure 3b). Target success remains 0/3 for scheduling and rises from 0/3 to 1/3 for the car case. In the car case, feedback confirms that flagging the pickup–car-use conflict before Day 23 preserves the pickup option pending household coordination, satisfying the target. In scheduling, the Day-22 inquiry restarts action, but the user-approved resolution is executed on Day 27, after the Day-22 deadline.

5.3 Permission: Correcting a False Rule

At one checkpoint in each of six worlds, Qwen3-Max receives an externally supplied incorrect no-contact note: retain the judgment, rewrite it with the same meaning, or correct it to distinguish inquiry from commitment. With world state, evidence, tools, resources, and actual permissions fixed, we measure accepted target-related inquiries over ten independent one-interaction repeats per checkpoint and condition.

Correcting the restriction restores permitted inquiry.

When the note follows the observed records, correction yields 60/60 accepted inquiries, versus 5/60 for retaining it and 8/60 for equivalent rewriting (Figure 3c). The second presentation tests a combined update: reordering records and explicitly releasing a temporary wait. Inquiry also recovers under this update with the false note retained. Across both presentations, 360 control windows with genuine no-contact rules produce no target-contact attempts (Appendix M).

6 Discussion and Conclusion

OptionWorld locates shortcomings in long-term assistance by connecting each unfinished target to its evidence, judgments, actions, and outcome. The main study reveals failures at different points in this process: accessing sources can leave problems unrecognized, grounded judgments can go without action, and accepted actions can leave coordination unfinished. These findings make follow-through, alongside information acquisition and retention, a central requirement for long-term assistants.

Memory can preserve a mistaken reason to wait alongside useful facts, connecting persistent early assumptions in dialogue (Laban et al., 2025) to cross-day inaction. Exploratory support tests further distinguish restarting progress from completing the task. Together, the results motivate tracking what remains unresolved after each reply or action, when to retry, and whether a waiting condition still applies, so that unfinished work reaches timely resolution or preserves the user’s options.

Limitations

The results characterize eight authored worlds, their shared interaction budgets, and the tested model-and-runner configurations. Semantic scores and primary-problem labels depend on judgments of evidence and action appropriateness; the appendices document the review procedures, source adjudications, and uncertainty analyses. The information and action experiments examine selected checkpoints with three repetitions per condition. Broader recovery estimates require additional tasks and repetitions. The supplied-note experiment isolates permission judgments through short-window inquiry; natural error formation and final task completion remain distinct evaluation targets.

Ethical Considerations

The synthetic scenarios involve housing, work, health, finance, and family coordination. Simulated performance does not establish safety for autonomous high-stakes deployment, which requires consent, privacy protection, human oversight, and means of appeal. Public exports omit credentials, private evaluator cards, and private case-level annotations associated with individual targets.

Appendix A Comparison with Related Benchmarks

Table 1 distinguishes the tasks an agent faces from the measurements used to explain its performance. The final column requires repeated success measurements on the same targets, such as passk\mathrm{pass}^{k}; score variance receives partial coverage because it does not identify which targets succeed repeatedly. Oracle-information or context-access tests receive partial coverage for facts in the decision input. Stage-wise scores receive partial coverage for judgment-to-outcome analysis when the stages are not traced for the same target.

π\pi-Bench explicitly scores whether agents uncover hidden requirements through inference or targeted questions (Zhang et al., 2026, Sections 3.3–3.5), so it receives full coverage for need discovery. Its separate proactivity and completeness scores distinguish uncovering requirements from satisfying them; our diagnostic columns additionally ask how each target’s available facts, judgments, actions, and outcome are linked.

PROBE scores document retrieval, bottleneck identification, and action specification separately (Pasternak et al., 2025, Section 3.1); this supports its full mark for access versus judgment. VibeLifeBench uses per-stage, cross-stage, and final checks, and reports each task’s mean, minimum, maximum, and score deviation over three runs (Studio and AI, 2026, Sections 2.2.5 and 3.2). These are adjacent to tracing a single hidden target’s judgment through to outcome and aligning its binary successes across runs. Claw-Anything reports pass3\mathrm{pass}^{3} and varies access to event streams and context scale (Lin et al., 2026, Sections 4.1–4.2), supporting a full mark for repeated success and partial coverage of the input-availability dimension.

In OptionWorld, the input measure asks whether each failed target’s designated facts are still present in its last decision before the deadline.

Appendix B World Construction and Task Coverage

The worlds are authored synthetic environments compiled into public records and evaluator specifications. Construction starts from four scenario-family modules that define eight personas and 192 distinct situations. Each situation specifies a threatened option, a relation between records, a responsible authority, and an unsafe action. These are authored inputs to a deterministic compiler, not tasks generated during evaluation.

The compiler creates dated records, sources, contacts, and daily events. It assigns evidence dependencies, intervention windows, permissions, and delayed feedback; adds benign records; and replaces descriptive identifiers with opaque ones.

The resulting public snapshot contains the records and executable procedures. Its paired private snapshot contains target identities, required evidence, and success conditions. The recorded runs bind both snapshots by hash, so reproduction uses the exact archived worlds.

What varies across tasks.

A single-record constraint can be discovered by inspecting one object; a cross-record conflict requires relating separately acquired records. Cross-day targets require retaining earlier facts, while missing-event targets require checking whether an expected event occurred. Clarification targets require obtaining an answer before taking a further step. Multi-party targets separate identifying an issue from obtaining the preferences or authorization needed to resolve it. These patterns produce different evidence and action dependencies within the same tool interface.

Worlds vary the frequency and placement of these patterns. Their 60-day streams include overlapping matters, benign records, delayed replies, and changes to ongoing processes. All eight base worlds use neutral missions in the main experiment.

Public evidence and evaluation boundaries.

Each of the 192 targets has an evidence certificate: a record linking its required public records, their availability, matter identity, deadline basis, and action pathway. The release checker recomputes these links from the final records. It also checks that target-relevant metadata has counterparts among benign records, so directory format alone does not identify a scored target. Record IDs are opaque; no target list is supplied in the main condition. These construction checks test the consistency of the specified task, whereas execution and semantic review assess whether the agent meets the specified conditions.

All eight base worlds pass the recorded construction checks, with 24 evidence certificates each. The reproduction guide identifies the authoring modules, compiler, final snapshots, and check summaries so each stage can be inspected separately.

Local paths for persistently unsolved targets.

Evaluator-guided checks reach a resolving simulator response for all 25 targets in a fixed reachability audit. Each target starts in a fresh runtime using its recorded world snapshot and specified public procedure. The fixed set includes all 24 targets with no success credit across the five API systems’ 15 observations, plus one target with success credit. The archive includes the check code and individual results. These checks establish individual target reachability, rather than joint completion under one shared budget. Main-study OPR measures completion of concurrent tasks under the world’s inspection, comparison, and daily-action limits.

Appendix C Main-Study Execution Settings

Table 5 reports the recorded model identifiers and execution routes. Below we specify the daily interaction procedure, resource allowances, and archived request formats.

Shared API procedure.

All 120 API trajectories use a neutral mission without named targets and sequential single-action tool calls. The runner starts a fresh conversation each day and carries forward memory, watchpoints, public feedback, and the current directory. Tool interactions accumulate within that day. Previously inspected material remains retrievable by its identifier. The model can finish a day before reaching the 16-turn limit; each response has a 4,096-token completion allowance. Memory summaries and watchpoint conditions are limited to 640 characters per entry and retain references to their supporting records.

Model routes and repeat settings.

The DeepSeek adapter sends deepseek-v4-pro to the official endpoint; Table 5 retains the versioned identifier recorded by the experiment. The other API systems use their listed OpenRouter IDs with a fixed provider route. Temperature and provider seed are omitted in all 120 trace configurations. Run labels identify repeats of the same worlds, not controlled provider random seeds. Astra runs through a separate local agent interface. The 720-window permission experiment uses Qwen3-Max; this is a different model from the one in the main-study Qwen slot.

On the Alibaba route, null assistant tool-message content is serialized as an empty string. All API trajectories use the same task prompt, tools, and environment budgets; archived configurations specify request formats.

C.1 Agent Instructions and Tool Interface

All 120 API trajectories share this system instruction and daily-reset rule. It comes from an archived request. Supplementary files retain the exact prompt and JSON tool schemas.

You are a long-term personal assistant. Review the information that becomes available each day and decide what, if anything, is useful to do. Use only information you have actually accessed. Respect the user’s authority, privacy, stated preferences, and attention. Seek confirmation before preference-bearing or irreversible commitments, and account for feedback that arrives later. Call exactly one tool in each assistant response. Use tools only when useful. Finish each day explicitly. Each simulated day starts a new conversation window. The packet’s public_event_history, memory, watchpoints, feedback, and archive ID lists are the persistent cross-day state. Previously opened sources and inspected objects may be reopened by archived ID without consuming the source/object attention budget.

The neutral mission supplied with the world is:

Support the user’s ongoing life administration using the records, preferences, and authorization boundaries available in the world. Maintain concise provenance-bearing notes when useful, minimize disclosure, respect later feedback, and request confirmation before preference-bearing commitments. No issue list or target task is supplied.

Daily input.

The initial request combines a stable prefix (persona, mission, horizon, budgets, and interaction policy) with the current day’s packet. The latter contains the public event stream and history, available source and object directories, stakeholders, archive IDs, saved memory, watchpoints, feedback, and remaining budgets. Directory entries do not replace opening a source or inspecting an object. Within the day, tool responses are appended to the conversation; the next day begins with a new packet. The exact packet key names are provided in the supplementary input-structure file.

Action tools can return a rejection instead of a receipt. A receipt confirms delivery or a state change, not the target outcome; outcome credit also requires the later feedback described below.

The runtime stores record_assessment as report_risk, and the two execution tools as commit_confirmed_intervention and commit_reversible_intervention. The selected trace excerpts retain both the submitted tool name and the runtime name when available.

Appendix D Semantic Review and Scoring Decisions

What the reviewers see.

Two LLM agents in separate contexts inspect identity-masked chronological records and anonymous target requirements. The material includes acquired evidence, failed actions, and nonterminal feedback; model identity, previous scores, and structured terminal outcome labels are withheld. Agent-authored text is preserved and may include descriptions of results. Reviewers identify action indices supporting recognition (HH), grounding (GG), and an appropriate external intervention. They may mark a judgment uncertain. Different action indices can express the same supported target-level judgment.

Reviewer configuration.

Reviewer models are distinct from the acting-system configurations in Appendix C. Archived launch records for the stage review specify gpt-6-sol, with gpt-6-luna used for designated assignments. These identifiers describe requested reviewer configurations. Each paired review uses separate contexts that do not share judgments, including pairs using the same model. The supplemental batch below measures agreement between these recorded reviews. Reviewer settings for the information and action follow-ups appear in Appendix L, alongside their endpoint definitions.

Reviewer instructions.

The frozen rubric instructs each reviewer to use only the assigned anonymous packet, inspect the full chronological action inventory, and cite evidence acquired strictly before each proposed witness: a specific action supporting the judgment and located by its trace index. Reviewers return a target identifier, action-index lists for HH, GG, and intervention eligibility, an uncertainty flag for each judgment, and an explanation of the evidence. All qualifying grounding and intervention witnesses must be listed, including follow-ups. Failed actions may support recognition or grounding but cannot establish delivery; each action can count toward only one independent target. The supplement contains the frozen review instructions and scoring definitions. The observation/recognition distinction is specified below.

From judgments to scores.

The scoring code checks that evidence precedes the cited action, grounding falls within the valid window, and an external action has an accepted delivery receipt. Paired reviews supply criterion-level judgments and action witnesses. Confirmed credit requires support from both reviews or a source-grounded adjudication of the disputed judgment. Adjudications identify the supporting actions and records; both reviews remain preserved. Unresolved disagreements retain their uncertainty status and enter the sensitivity analysis.

Evidence references are read from each tool’s schema: evidence_ids for ordinary actions, provenance for memory, and source_scope for watchpoints. All reported results use the same finalized scoring records, described in Appendix J.1.

Once reviews are sealed, the code joins outcome feedback to the same action receipt and target. Reports, reminders, and saved notes can support recognition or grounding, but delivery requires an accepted external action.

Observation and recognition.

OO records a successful access to a target’s designated source or object, including a qualifying comparison. HH records specific problem recognition supported by information available before the witness action. Initial user messages and daily public events can therefore support HH without OO. Four target instances have O=0,H=1O=0,H=1: two Grok Run-1 targets, one Fable Run-1 target, and one DeepSeek Run-2 target. Their later criteria are zero. The remaining order is H≥G≥T≥I≥YH\geq G\geq T\geq I\geq Y. Counts such as observed-but-unrecognized targets are computed directly from the joint labels (O=1O=1, H=0H=0).

Human review.

Multiple human reviewers examined all 144 main-study trajectories. For failure classification, they checked every initial LLM classification against the underlying trajectory, resolved disagreements, and finalized the labels. The review coverage and procedure are described in supplement/human_review_statement.json. The worked examples trace target-level decisions through archived actions and sealed LLM judgments; reviewer agreement is computed from paired LLM decisions.

Reviewer consistency.

The supplemental batch supplies two finalized reviews for each of 33 trajectories: eight DeepSeek Run-2 trajectories, one Fable Run-3 trajectory, and all 24 Astra trajectories. Table 8 compares the 792 paired target decisions in this batch. We classify each raw semantic decision as supported, unsupported, or uncertain, before combining reviews and applying timing and receipt checks. The other 111 trajectories have paired judgments outside this agreement batch.

D.1 Worked Main-Study Example

DeepSeek’s second run in the independent-contractor world provides a complete scoring sequence. The receipt specifies a commercial software plan, while the console shows a personal plan. An expected follow-up is absent from the ledger at Day 8. The relevant intervention window is Days 8–16. Table 9 follows the acquired records, initial request, revision, and linked outcome.

All six final criteria are satisfied, with no uncertainty in either review. Both reviewers accept actions 62 and 97 as interventions; only action 97 links to qualifying outcome feedback. The example distinguishes accepted delivery (II) from simulator-confirmed resolution (YY).

D.2 Contrasting Scoring Decisions

Table 10 contrasts this success with four decisions from the same trajectory. These examples illustrate the scoring rules. Outcome credit requires an action appropriate for the target and feedback establishing the required outcome.

The work-limit case enters the sensitivity analysis with uncertain II and YY labels under the scoring rule above.

supplement/scoring_decision_examples.json preserves both original opinions, selected action records, final criterion labels, and source hashes for all five cases. The full-record archive can regenerate this file from the sealed records without a new model call.

D.3 From Rejection to a Waiting Condition

The Qwen rent example in Section 4.2 comes from Run 3 in the retired-tenant world. On Day 19, a process lookup returns a reversible route with a Day 26 deadline. The attempted action is then rejected. Table 11 shows the model’s interpretation and its later use in the original main-study trace.

The rejection does not require another record. The model introduces that condition, saves it, and cites the record’s absence five days later as the reason for not retrying.

Appendix E Full API Comparison

Table 12 reports the six criteria across all eight worlds and three runs, using the same rubric for every API system. Tables 13 and 14 provide the API-system counts in Figure 2: repeated outcomes on the same targets and failures grouped by timely primary-fact acquisition.

DeepSeek succeeds at least once on 149 distinct targets; the other four systems add 19, for 168/192 targets overall. Each target has 15 observations across five systems and three runs. Twenty-four targets never succeed. Only one succeeds in all 15.

Appendix F Complete Outcome Inventory

Table 15 gives all six criterion counts and OPR for each system and run, underlying the averages in Table 2. Because every run contains 192 targets, each mean percentage also equals the pooled rate across the system’s 576 target instances. Table 16 gives outcomes for every world and run, each with 24 targets. The machine-readable export contains one row per trajectory, including its execution setting and all six criterion counts.
