Appendix G World-Level Robustness

Do the system comparisons depend on which worlds are included? Each world contributes 24 targets observed in three runs. We resample eight whole worlds with replacement, retaining all targets and runs within each draw. For paired comparisons, both systems receive the same draws. The computation enumerates all 88=16,777,2168^{8}=16{,}777{,}216 ordered resamples through 6,435 multiplicity vectors, weighted by their multinomial counts. Interval endpoints are the exact 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of this distribution. Table 17 separates variation across the three runs from sensitivity to which worlds are sampled.

DeepSeek’s pooled lead over each other API system remains positive when any one world is removed. It leads Fable in six worlds, with one tie, Gemini in seven, Grok in eight, and Qwen in five. Its paired lead over Qwen is 12.5 points, with a resampling interval of 2.4–22.4; removing one world at a time leaves a lead of 9.3–15.1 points. The corresponding leave-one-world-out ranges against Fable, Gemini, and Grok are 9.3–14.9, 15.7–20.8, and 20.0–27.0 points.

These intervals quantify sensitivity to the eight authored worlds, conditional on the recorded labels and runs. Review uncertainty is examined separately in Appendix H. This post-hoc descriptive analysis compares the pooled-leading system with each other API system.

Appendix H Review Sensitivity

Do the reported patterns change when uncertain judgments are scored differently? Table 18 changes every unsuccessful target with any stage-level uncertainty to success, leaving all others unchanged. The resulting upper bound includes uncertainty in any criterion, including disagreements that do not directly concern the outcome.

Table 19 applies the same stress test to the repeat counts in Table 13. Removing all triplets with any uncertain judgment leaves 538 system–target groups: 582 of their 883 failed instances recur in all three runs (65.9%). Relabelling every uncertain failure as successful gives 582/1,309 (44.5%). Both analyses recompute the repeated-failure share on the recorded runs, using exclusion and success assignment as two explicit treatments of uncertainty in the recorded scores.

Appendix I Facts Available at Decision Time

Primary-fact acquisition requires inspection or comparison to return each designated fact before the target’s deadline. This differs from source access (OO), which can expose a relevant source without its required fields. The input-visibility analysis then asks whether those acquired facts remain available at the last valid decision.

Runs 2–3 retain 46,606 pre-action requests or bridge payloads across 96 trajectories: 41,285 API requests and 5,321 Astra bridge inputs. Every retained action in this mapping has an associated input, including actions from recovered continuation segments. The API cohort contains all 80 trajectories from Runs 2–3 and 1,920 targets, including 1,295 failures. Astra’s 16 later local runs remain a separate execution cohort.

For each target, we search the actual non-system input for each designated record’s primary fact, requiring the associated object or matter identifier. Matching normalizes case and whitespace; a catalog listing alone does not qualify. We use the last request within the target’s valid window so that later evidence cannot count as information available before its deadline.

At the last valid-window request, 460 API failures retain matches for all designated primary facts and their matter identifiers. Excluding all stage-uncertain targets leaves 1,545 targets, 920 failures, and 310 last-window matches (33.7%).

Appendix J Model Differences and Strategy Reuse

J.1 Full-Population Failure Classification

Population and unit.

The review covers all 2,096 target instances with Y=0Y=0 in the reported scoring snapshot: 1,875 from the five API systems and 221 from Astra (Codex). One instance is a model–run–world–target combination. We set aside 160 instances with normal constraints from the model-error classification, leaving 1,936 instances: 1,524 with a specific observed problem and 412 with insufficient attribution evidence. Main-result denominators remain unchanged; classification does not itself alter outcome scores. Table 23 lists exclusions and evidence coverage for each system.

One primary observed problem per instance.

LLM reviewers produced the initial classifications from the existing reviews and adjudications. Human reviewers checked each classification against the original actions and feedback, resolved disagreements, and finalized the labels. The primary label identifies the documented obstacle still blocking the target. When several problems appear, an explicit unsupported prerequisite can explain subsequent inaction, while a repaired parameter error does not displace a remaining obstacle. Each instance receives one primary label; the five problem types are:

  • •

    Self-restriction: an unsupported prerequisite or expanded prohibition is explicitly used to wait, refuse, or restrict progress.

  • •

    State or updating error: a wrong matter, date, source, or status is used in a decision, or a superseded judgment continues to govern it.

  • •

    Action selection or adjustment: the record establishes a permitted opportunity, but the agent fails to take the available action, retry, follow up, or try another approach.

  • •

    Execution error: an identifiable agent-side parameter, binding, ordering, or procedure error obstructs the selected operation and remains relevant to progress.

  • •

    Information gap: needed facts are not obtained, assembled, or retained in time, without evidence for a more specific primary problem.

Insufficient evidence is a separate status retained in every category-share denominator, so the reported shares describe the full classification set. It includes missing decision records and ambiguous action or scoring interpretations that prevent selection of a primary problem. Fixed quota exhaustion or a genuine permission limit alone does not establish model error. Conversely, a rejected request does not justify exclusion when a documented model mistake or unused permitted alternative explains the blockage.

Evidence and review.

Each classification retains its target identity, reason, source records, and event references where applicable. Public rules and agent-visible information establish the relevant constraints; private target definitions do not show that the agent had access to the same information.

User authorization does not by itself resolve conflicting objective facts. A completed procedure can therefore still contain an unsupported state choice. Outcome scoring follows the simulated feedback under the target criteria in Section 3.2.

The initial synthesis combines model identities, offline agent reviews, and recorded adjudications. The full-confirmation review log records separately launched gpt-6.1-sol contexts with fork_context=false for its assigned evidence checks. Retained review submissions and source-grounded adjudications inform the final labels.

Scoring records.

Both the main results and failure labels use the same finalized scoring records. Unresolved stage-level scoring judgments retain their uncertainty flags. The records include source hashes and action witnesses. The reproduction procedure in Appendix N uses these target-level records.

Astra: acknowledging uncertainty while choosing a date.

In two returning-worker runs, Astra acknowledges an unresolved date conflict but selects and executes one date. The active records state Day 21 and Day 26. In Run 2, the Day-9 confirmation request explicitly says that neither consultation establishes which date is correct, while its proposed action asks to use Day 21 and align the portal to it. On Day 12, the agent executes that confirmation-bound action. Run 3 similarly states that the consultations do not establish which date governs, then proposes and executes the Day-21 choice (Run 2 indices 59 and 88; Run 3 indices 62 and 95 in the corresponding returning-worker timelines). User approval authorizes a change, but does not establish which conflicting date is correct: the agent chooses a date while acknowledging that the evidence does not settle the conflict.

J.2 Stage Profiles and Strategy Reuse

Models differ in where they fall short.

The stage counts distinguish failure to recognize a problem from failure to act on a timely judgment. Gemini has 180 cases with accessed evidence but no specific hypothesis. Grok has 128/289 timely judgments without eligible delivery (44.3%), compared with 121/450 (26.9%) for DeepSeek.

Multi-party targets expose a further gap between recognition and outcome. DeepSeek’s high overall observation and recognition coverage (556 and 497 of 576) accompanies its larger outcome count. On multi-party targets, however, it recognizes 103/105 risks while grounding 79 and achieving 22 outcomes. Fable completes 45/96 clarification targets and 17/105 multi-party tasks.

Task pathways after timely discovery.

To compare completion after recognition, we retain API instances with T=1T=1 and no uncertain stage judgments. All retained instances also have timely primary facts. Success counts are 264/291 for missing expected events, 143/209 for single-source constraints, 153/254 for cross-day accumulation, 172/231 for cross-source conflicts, 179/232 for stakeholder clarification, and 94/246 for preference or multi-party tasks. In particular, obtaining and understanding the required evidence does not make single-source tasks the easiest to complete.

The construction links these evidence patterns to different action routes: missing-event tasks use a responsible-party resolution route, while cross-day tasks require confirmed execution. The comparison therefore describes complete task pathways rather than isolating a memory effect. In Grok’s Run-1 retired-tenant trajectory, a request to the responsible institution completes a benefit-renewal matter on Days 10–11 (target 01-02, trace indices 80, 84). For a tax-declaration matter (01-03), it compares the records and recognizes the conflict on Day 14 (107–112), but delivers no qualifying intervention by Day 23. These two instances have timely primary facts and grounded judgments, with no uncertain stage labels, yet differ in outcomes after discovery.

Coverage differences matter for model comparisons.

Direct inspection has a horizon quota of 46, whereas each world releases 68–71 records. Comparison can return new facts without another direct inspection. Table 25 compares outcomes on the same 311 target instances whose primary facts all five API systems obtain in time. Removing targets with any system’s review uncertainty leaves 139 instances. Relative outcome counts change with this shared-access selection. This comparison measures success with shared fact access; the full-cohort ranking also captures fact acquisition.

The 239-instance DeepSeek–Grok comparison requires timely fact acquisition by both systems and excludes targets with either system’s uncertain criterion labels. Qualifying interventions number 185 and 127, respectively. Thus, the delivery gap is also present among instances where both systems obtain the designated facts and neither has an uncertain criterion label.

What stage separation reveals.

Stage combinations describe breaks in progress and may overlap; they are distinct from the mutually exclusive primary-problem labels. Across the five API systems, 652 of 2,880 target instances have O=1,H=0O=1,H=0, showing that source access can stop short of recognizing a specific risk. Another 470 have T=1,I=0T=1,I=0: a timely, grounded judgment does not lead to a qualifying intervention. The gap after delivery is concentrated in preference, authorization, and multi-party targets: these account for 103 of the 170 cases with I=1,Y=0I=1,Y=0 (60.6%) but only 525 of 2,880 instances (18.2%). Within these task types, 418 risk judgments (79.6%) yield 94 outcomes (17.9%).

Table 24 separates evidence and action dependencies by target type. For single-source, cross-source, and cross-day targets, all qualifying delivered interventions have matching outcomes in the observed runs: their combined 1,410 instances contain no I=1,Y=0I=1,Y=0 case. Missing-event, clarification, and preference/multi-party targets contribute 12, 55, and 103 such cases, respectively. The criteria expose where task pathways differ.

Checkpoint evidence for strategy reuse.

The fixed stratified sample contains two randomly selected failures per API system and world, for 80 targets across five systems and eight worlds. The sample was drawn from the 1,739 failed target instances in the 111-trajectory screening cohort. The review combines target traces, archived judgments, input checks, and checkpoint replays. Each replay uses the corresponding public object identifiers and remaining comparison allowance; the original day-close operation is also reproduced. Each replay tests whether the missing facts could be acquired from that target’s original state using the resources still available.

Among the 35 targets missing primary facts, 15 have successful comparison replays at checkpoints 5–10 days before their deadlines: six Fable, three Gemini, two Grok, and four Qwen cases. Five of these trajectories previously acquired fresh facts by comparison (three Fable and two Gemini cases).

Table 26 records the resources at these checkpoints. All 15 have exhausted the 46-object inspection allowance but retain an unused daily comparison slot and 9–22 remaining horizon comparisons. Direct access fails under the original quotas; comparison returns the missing primary facts 5–10 days before the deadline. It is an information-only operation with no user commitment. For example, Fable’s contractor run has 14 comparisons left on Day 49, before a Day 57 deadline. Comparing the two public object IDs returns the conflict between a requested public showreel and an NDA forbidding public excerpts. The same trajectory had obtained fresh facts through comparison on Day 40.

The replay endpoint is fact retrieval at each target’s original checkpoint. The 15 successful replays therefore establish individually available alternatives, with resources evaluated separately at each checkpoint. Aggregate counts, checkpoint resource summaries, and source hashes are in results/acquisition_adaptation.json and results/replay_feasibility.json.

J.3 Astra and DeepSeek: Discovery to Action

Matched timely judgments.

We match instances by run, world, and target, retaining those with T=1T=1 and no uncertain stage judgments for either system. This yields 275 instances: Astra has 268 qualifying interventions and 262 successes, versus DeepSeek’s 227 and 207. Both systems have already made timely, evidence-supported judgments on these same instances, placing the remaining difference in intervention and completion. These counts complement Table 2’s full-cohort rates.

A shared discrepancy, different next steps.

In Run 2 of the returning-to-work caregiver world, both systems inspect a claimant commitment allowing 24 hours of availability on Day 3 and a portal assignment of 35 search hours on Day 7. Both recognize the conflict. Astra requests confirmation on Day 7 to submit a correction request, while preserving both records and leaving factual reconciliation to the responsible record holder. It executes the confirmed action on Day 8; Day-9 environment feedback confirms option preservation, not resolution of the conflicting records. DeepSeek saves the discrepancy and registers a watchpoint on Day 7, waiting for the record holder to become available, but delivers no qualifying intervention for this target. The difference is how recognized uncertainty guides the next step: Astra uses an authorized protective action without claiming to have settled the facts; DeepSeek retains the conflict as a monitoring condition. The archived target is risk-caregiver_returning_to_work-01-02. Evidence appears at Astra trace indices 17, 41, 44, 49, and 56, and DeepSeek indices 24, 61, 71, and 72; indices are zero-based in the Run-2 traces mapped by main_manifest.json in the reproduction archive.

What a harness explanation would test.

Both setups have a harness: the execution framework that supplies context, dispatches tools, and returns feedback to the model. The common runner starts a new conversation each day, carrying saved memory and watchpoints; Astra uses the local Codex agent interface. Codex’s documented harness manages conversation state and tool execution across turns (Bonamy and Choi, 2026). This makes continuity of pending steps and use of action feedback plausible contributors to follow-through. The observed comparison changes both the model and its harness, so it describes their combined behavior. A same-model comparison across harnesses would isolate whether these execution features improve follow-through; the case above identifies concrete behaviors to test: turning a recognized conflict into an authorized action and checking its outcome.

J.4 Paired Trajectories After Recognition

The following comparisons link current outcome labels to actions in the archived traces. Each cited instance has timely primary facts, a timely grounded judgment, and no uncertain stage labels. Trace indices are zero-based and include feedback events; main_manifest.json maps each run, system, and world to its archived trace.

Grok and DeepSeek: monitoring versus authorized execution.

In Run 3 of the food-business world, a supplier credit memo conflicts with a scheduled full debit (target risk-neighborhood_food_business_owner-03-02, deadline Day 32). Grok obtains the records on Days 12 and 24, looks up the confirmation-based procedure, then saves the discrepancy, a watchpoint, and a risk report on Day 24 (indices 81, 170–176). DeepSeek obtains the same facts (141, 328), requests confirmation on Day 24 (332), receives it on Day 25 (339), and executes on Day 27 (384), followed by preservation feedback on Day 28 (397). Across the three runs, Grok never completes this target while DeepSeek completes it each time. Grok’s surface behavior varies: Run 1 acts after the deadline, Run 2 records a reminder without an external state change, and Run 3 monitors the conflict. Different action sequences can thus yield the same persistent failure.

Fable and Qwen: equal totals, opposite task outcomes.

Across 576 matched instances, both succeed in 132, only Fable in 76, only Qwen in 74, and neither in 294. Requiring timely primary facts and no uncertain stage labels for both leaves 249 instances: 132 joint successes, 37 Fable-only, 41 Qwen-only, and 39 joint failures. Thus, both systems obtain timely facts in 78 of the 150 full-cohort disagreements.

Two Run-1 caregiver tasks illustrate the two directions. The target IDs in this world share the prefix risk-caregiver_returning_to_work; the suffixes below identify each matter. For the care allowance discrepancy (03-02), Fable consults both parties on Days 25–26, requests confirmation on Day 27, and follows up on Day 29 after no response. Confirmation and execution occur on Day 30, before the Day-37 deadline (indices 228–285). Qwen’s confirmation request precedes completed consultation and is rejected; later contact attempts are also rejected. It saves a condition requiring fresh instructions before retrying and does not complete the target (319–323, 374–376, 407, 508).

The direction reverses for a childcare funding code that covers autumn but appears against a summer-session charge (01-03). Fable recognizes the mismatch on Day 13 and waits for another record or invoice amount before contacting the provider (97–102). Qwen contacts the provider on Day 13, follows up after a partial reply on Day 16, receives clarification on Day 17, and intervenes on Day 18 before the Day-22 deadline (166–257). Both trajectories finish 12 of 24 targets; their identical totals conceal different choices about follow-up on these two matters.

DeepSeek across runs: stable discovery, variable next steps.

For caregiver target 03-03, all three runs identify a pension statement recording seven years of service and a conflicting zero-service quote, with a Day-36 deadline. Runs 1 and 2 use the reversible procedure to preserve the service record without deciding which entry governs: interventions occur on Days 27 and 28, with next-day feedback (Run 1 indices 348, 351, 352, 360; Run 2 indices 363, 365, 378, 386). Run 3 obtains the discrepancy and the same available procedure on Day 27 (388, 390), but saves a watchpoint awaiting another record (394). Its Day-36 memory still treats the matter as pending (506), and no qualifying intervention occurs. Here repeat inconsistency lies in using an available protective action after consistently recognizing the problem.

DeepSeek’s mortgage case: accepted execution, different outcomes.

The 122-instance coordination subset requires timely primary facts and grounded judgment, no uncertain stage labels, completed consultations with both required parties, a user-approved action, and accepted execution by the deadline. Of these instances, 94 succeed; among the 28 failures, 21 receive intervention credit but not outcome credit, and seven receive neither. Accepted execution and a qualifying intervention are therefore separate checks.

The mortgage example is target 03-02 in the midcareer_worker_after_layoff world. In Run 1, DeepSeek proposes asking the loss-mitigation office to apply the hardship pause on Day 26 (356), obtains confirmation and executes on Day 27 (366, 370), with feedback on Day 28 (386). In Run 2 it instead proposes treating the letter as controlling and pausing the debit itself on Day 27 (395), then obtains confirmation and executes on Day 28 (408, 410). Although execution is accepted and feedback arrives (434), the action does not satisfy the target’s requirements. Both runs complete consultation and authorization; the outcome differs with the proposed resolution of the conflicting payment instructions.

Explicit feedback supports local revision.

We identify each API target instance’s first material-return or partial-resolution feedback, using the operation or matter identifier and linked transaction IDs to associate events with the target. Eligibility requires that the feedback arrive by the deadline and that its specified follow-up day be no later than that deadline. It does not require a later request or successful outcome. An accepted follow-up is a subsequent contact on or after the allowed day and by the deadline, explicitly citing the feedback ID and receiving a request_logged response.

Of 102 material-return and 134 partial-resolution instances, 99 and 126 meet these timing conditions. All eligible instances have an accepted follow-up; the current target outcomes are successful in 91/99 and 109/126, respectively. Restricting further to timely primary facts, T=1T=1, and no uncertain stage labels yields 95 and 113 instances, again all with accepted follow-ups, and 91 and 109 successes. These feedback messages specify the missing case_reference field, the revision format, and the requirement to bind its value to an inspected source. The result characterizes repair within these explicitly guided interactions.

In Grok’s Run-1 contractor trajectory, the licensing correction target 01-02 illustrates the sequence. On Day 8, Grok receives notice that user confirmation is unnecessary and switches to contacting the responsible desk (indices 68–69). The Day-9 return specifies the missing field (73). Grok rereads the records on Day 10 (84–85), submits the field value with its source and feedback reference (92), and receives resolution feedback on Day 11 (100). Its current outcome label is successful and has no uncertain stage judgment. This successful repair distinguishes responding to explicit correction instructions from deciding independently when and how to restart unfinished work.

Appendix K Resource Use and Temporal Patterns

More calls can maintain pending work rather than complete it.

Across all three runs and eight worlds, Fable makes 8,049 tool calls for 208 successes and Qwen makes 12,553 for 206. Table 27 breaks down every counted call by tool. Counts include attempted calls, errors, and day-close calls; they exclude environment feedback, protocol recovery events, and forced day closures. These are tool attempts, not provider requests or costs.

Risk reporting and watchpoint registration account for 1,967 of Qwen’s 4,504 additional calls (43.7%). Procedure lookups add 844 and inspections 754; the remaining tools together add 939. Reporting and monitoring help retain unresolved matters, but their repetition does not itself deliver the next external action. Qwen also makes more contact and intervention attempts, showing why call counts must be read alongside acceptance, timing, and target outcomes. Fable uses fewer calls in all 24 matched world–run pairs, yet has more successes in nine, fewer in ten, and the same number in five. The resource difference is consistent across these pairs, whereas outcome superiority is not.

Resource totals and later tasks.

In Run 3, Qwen uses 196.6 million recorded input tokens and 4,257 tool calls for 76 successes; DeepSeek uses 145.6 million and 4,087 calls for 109. This cross-model comparison aggregates all eight worlds; input totals include retransmitted context. These totals describe resource use and outcomes under each system’s model and action policy. Higher resource use can accompany lower success; the number of interactions alone does not indicate whether they advance unfinished tasks.

We next examine when tasks become detectable and whether failures follow budget exhaustion. We group targets by earliest detection day: early (Days 1–20), middle (21–40), and late (41–60). Late-target success is lower than early-target success in 14 of 15 model–run groups. DeepSeek Run 3 is the exception, with 31/59 early-target successes and 28/46 late-target successes.

Inspection capacity is depleted before late targets appear.

Counting successful budget-consuming inspections, rather than rejection messages, shows that all 120 API trajectories use their 46 direct inspections by Days 31–39. Free retrievals of previously inspected records do not enter this count. All 690 late-onset API instances therefore become detectable after this allowance is exhausted. Yet 88 of the 120 trajectories record no horizon-level read/inspect rejection: an agent that stops trying after exhaustion produces no such error. For example, Qwen’s Run-1 laid-off-worker trajectory consumes its 46th inspection on Day 32 (index 463) and records on Day 42 that newly arrived records cannot be inspected with the remaining allowance (575), without a horizon-level rejection.

Gemini records such rejections in 16/24 trajectories; targets appearing after its first rejection have 8/112 outcomes, versus 169/464 otherwise. This is an association with attempts made after depletion, not a division between exhausted and unexhausted trajectories. Direct inspection and other operations have separate budgets: record comparison provides another route to new facts, as the checkpoint replays in Appendix J.2 demonstrate.

Late failures differ in fact-acquisition coverage.

Each API system has 177 early and 138 late target instances across its three runs. All 177 early instances have timely primary facts in each system. Among late instances, DeepSeek obtains those facts for 108/138, compared with 12/138 for Fable, 19/138 for Gemini, 6/138 for Grok, and 3/138 for Qwen. The latter four systems lack timely primary facts in 512 of 526 late failures (97.3%); excluding any uncertain stage labels leaves 372 of 381 (97.6%). DeepSeek lacks them in 30 of its 77 late failures. Thus much of the late deficit in those four systems is located at fact acquisition, whereas DeepSeek more often reaches a later stage. The time comparison spans changing information-access conditions and task mixes; it does not isolate deterioration in memory. Fact availability still does not ensure completion: in DeepSeek’s Run-1 laid-off-worker trajectory, target 06-01 has its primary facts by Day 42 (index 576), before the Day-49 deadline, but receives T=1,I=0,Y=0T=1,I=0,Y=0 under the current criteria.

Appendix L Information and Action Follow-ups: Protocol and Checks

These experiments test recovery at selected natural-failure checkpoints: task completion after information support, and timely intervention and task completion after action reminders.

Information outcomes across conditions.

All 18 supported continuations receive the designated primary facts: ten succeed, two are confirmed failures without a qualifying next step, and six have uncertain outcome scores. At Run-2 training, the six supported continuations yield one failure and five unknowns. Reformatting yields 2/3 successes at both responsive checkpoints, versus 3/3 with added facts. Seven outcomes remain unknown across all 27 information continuations.

L.1 Checkpoints and Selection

Both experiments resume archived natural-failure states, generating fresh continuations for every condition, including the controls. Table 29 identifies the five checkpoints. All 39 scheduled continuations reach Day 60; none stops upon focal success. Target windows, permissions, budgets, model routes, and scoring rules are unchanged.

Information selection.

The roster consists of three previously qualified retrieval paths, fixed before new outputs. Each checkpoint lacks primary facts that a permitted native comparison can retrieve. The two training checkpoints share one world–target pair; together with the buyout case they form two clusters. This purposive selection tests targeted acquisition of previously unobserved facts and whether supplying them restores progress on the original task.

Action selection.

A frozen screen starts from 412 records carrying the action-selection label in the screening snapshot. Recorded descriptions assign provisional strata for omission, follow-up/retry, and route adjustment; retrieval-related and unclassified descriptions do not enter those strata. A stratified hash rule selects 12, with at most one per source trajectory, before checking the archived state for a remaining permitted opportunity.

Admission requires six conditions at the exact restart boundary: the relevant facts are present in the decision input; the agent has expressed the correct interpretation; its understanding of the current state and permissions is correct; a substantive permitted next action is available; no unsupported restriction is driving the pause; and sufficient time and resources remain. These checkpoint conditions isolate the opportunity for an action reminder. The historical classification concerns the trajectory’s observed problem, whereas admission concerns the state from which the experiment will resume.

Two candidates meet all six conditions. For nine, the archived input and pre-action state cannot be jointly bound, or the available record does not establish the required interpretation, permission, or remaining action window. One is excluded because the agent explicitly infers a private-reminder-only restriction from the process response, placing an unsupported permission judgment upstream of inaction. The two-case roster is fixed before continuation outputs are generated. The food-business case concerns following up when a contact is available; the car case concerns progress after daily capacity returns. Further process lookups may still be needed to identify the procedural fields required for the next action.

L.2 Interventions and Resource Accounting

Information support.

The added facts and reformatted facts conditions correspond to raw support and transposed support, respectively, in the archived protocol. We use the descriptive names throughout the tables. Original continuations receive no added evidence. Both support conditions execute one researcher-selected, read-only compare_objects operation on the relevant public record pair. The added-facts condition supplies the returned facts and a literal table. The reformatted-facts condition exchanges the table’s rows and columns without changing its cells. Neither condition explains the discrepancy or supplies a plan for the next action.

Normal comparison and daily-action charges apply; the two support conditions share the resulting state. Additional prompt tokens are charged; researcher selection effort is not included in model cost. The primary added-facts versus original contrast tests the package of targeted retrieval, evidence availability, salience, and its resource use. The secondary reformatted-facts versus added-facts contrast tests only presentation.

The acquired evidence is presented as environment-provided information in a user message. Appending this evidence leaves earlier messages and model signatures unchanged.

Action reminders.

Each reminder is appended once as a user message at the admitted boundary; the native next-day reset remains unchanged. Both share this opening instruction:

Review unfinished matters using the information currently available, remaining resources, and existing authorization limits. This reminder adds no facts, permissions, or resources.

General review continues:

Consider the current situation and unresolved matters, assess what remains appropriate under existing conditions, then choose your next step.

Action review instead continues:

Check whether permitted follow-up, retry after a lifted restriction, or another lawful approach is appropriate, then choose your next step.

The comparison estimates the effect of action review relative to general review at each checkpoint; general review is the control condition. Results remain separate for each model–case combination.

L.3 Scoring and Uncertainty

Original endpoints.

The information experiment’s primary endpoint is the original target outcome YY; the action experiment’s is a new post-checkpoint timely, grounded intervention II, with YY secondary. The controlled information comparison never counts as an autonomous qualifying intervention. Success requires the original evidence, timing, authority, and outcome checks, not merely an accepted tool call. YY can mean preserving an option pending resolution, even while the underlying issue awaits a final resolution.

Each of the 39 joined prefix–continuation histories is evaluated by two separately launched AI review contexts, both configured as gpt-6.1-sol with high reasoning effort and fork_context=false. Acting-model and condition labels are withheld; neither context receives the other’s judgments. Source checks by the organizing AI agent and the original scoring program follow. The intervention text itself remains visible in the history. These 78 accepted AI reviews each check all 24 targets and post-checkpoint authority attempts. The final review pairs are sealed, with source hashes checked for each pair.

Seven unknown information outcomes.

Six involve whether a training-hours request merely asks an authority to reconcile 400 versus 720 hours, or assumes eligibility for 720 without establishing the required supervisory proof. The remaining case concerns whether a multi-target daily summary establishes focal risk recognition (HH). The frozen dependency rules preserve this upstream uncertainty. All seven remain in the fixed denominators. The action experiment has resolved judgments for every focal II and YY outcome.

Analysis units.

Per-checkpoint counts are the primary presentation. The prespecified information summary first equally weights checkpoints within a world–target pair, then equally weights the two pairs. Assigning unresolved endpoints their worst and best values on the fixed continuations bounds each contrast. Added facts exceeds original continuation by +66.7+66.7 to +91.7+91.7 percentage points; the increment from reformatting ranges from −41.7-41.7 to +8.3+8.3 points. Three repetitions characterize within-checkpoint variation. Information and action results describe recovery at the selected checkpoints.

L.4 Execution and Secondary Checks

Complete histories, including unsuccessful actions.

The information experiment contains 27 continuations and 1,084 requests; the action experiment contains 12 continuations and 4,176 requests. Result and cost totals cover these 39 analyzed continuations. All 27 information-experiment terminal states are accounted for, and recorded state replay passes. Seven explicit no-action responses (three malformed-function responses and four token-limit responses) remain in the record. Continuations use the bounded protocol recovery and a 4,096-token output limit, retaining saved responses.

What recovery looks like in the traces.

  • •

    Scheduling. In the scheduling action condition, a Day-22 inquiry about the inspection–pickup overlap qualifies as new II. The agent executes the user-approved resolution on Day 27 and receives feedback on Day 28. Outcome credit depends on the protective operation’s actual date, which falls after the Day-22 deadline.

  • •

    Shared car. On Day 19, the agent applies a reversible flag to the overlap between the clinic pickup and the grandson’s car-use period, leaving both records unchanged. Day-20 feedback confirms that the pickup option is preserved pending household coordination.

  • •

    Buyout. In four continuations, a Day-46 process lookup returns the authorized recipient’s identifier. The recipient becomes available on Day 47: contacting that identifier on Day 46 returns unknown stakeholder, and retrying on Day 47 produces an accepted request. Thus, discovering whom to contact precedes being able to contact them. The accepted retry then provides the receipt required for delivery credit.

Authority and other targets.

Table 30 reports all conditions. Information continuations have no confirmed unauthorized attempts, but 24 remain unresolved across 692 reviewed actor actions. Action continuations include confirmed unauthorized attempts in both reminder conditions. Normal quota errors alone do not count as authority violations.

For the other 23 targets, independent full-history reviews also reassess unresolved judgments in the shared pre-intervention history; resulting label differences need not reflect intervention effects. All prespecified other-outcome contrasts have uncertainty ranges spanning negative and positive values.

Costs and availability.

Provider-reported information-continuation cost is US$31.0364. The action experiment reports US$35.5638 for Gemini; DeepSeek has no provider-reported charge and a frozen-tariff upper bound of US$22.3435. These figures cover actor-model requests in the analyzed continuations; researcher curation and evaluation reviews are outside this cost scope.

Appendix N describes the aggregate exports and the full-record recovery archive, including access and public-copy transformations.

Appendix M Constraint Intervention: Protocol and Checkpoint Results

M.1 Design and Outcome Checks

Does correcting a supplied permission judgment restore an allowed inquiry? At six checkpoints from six worlds, Qwen3-Max receives one of three externally supplied notes that retain the incorrect no-contact judgment, rewrite it with the same meaning, or correct it to distinguish inquiry from commitment. Rewriting tests whether new wording suffices; correction changes the permission judgment. Within each presentation and permission setting, we hold the world, evidence, tools, resources, and actual permissions fixed.

We also test whether subsequent updates restore action while the false note remains. The current-state and update presentations jointly vary record order and a temporary waiting instruction that is explicitly released before action. Their exact input sequences appear below.

Each window is an independent interaction from a checkpoint. Six checkpoints, three note forms, two presentations, two permission settings, and ten repeats yield 720 windows. Half permit inquiry but prohibit commitments; half also prohibit contact. We count accepted target-related clarification inquiries to authorized recipients. Each plotted count pools six checkpoints and ten repeats for a total of 60 independent windows per plotted count.

Section 5.3 and Figure 3c report the pooled results; Table 31 separates them by checkpoint. Across the experiment, no preference-bearing commitment is executed; two confirmation-required state-change attempts are rejected.

M.2 Checkpoint Selection and Protocol

Table 31 separates the pooled counts in Figure 3c by checkpoint and condition.

Six checkpoints were selected before collecting new model outputs. Eligibility required public evidence for a permitted inquiry and an offline execution check of both its acceptance and the no-contact control. Table 31 maps each checkpoint to its tested matter. In four cases, this differs from the matter initially examined in the source snapshot.

Historical notes.

The common input presents the note as an earlier diagnostic judgment. Notes have Boolean fields contact_now and commitment_now, plus a summary. The commitment field is false in every condition. Contact is false in the retain and rewrite notes, and true in the corrected note when inquiry is allowed. Each note also includes the following summary text:

  • •

    Retain: “No contact permitted: approval for a preference-bearing commitment is still missing. No commitment allowed under the current user directive.”

  • •

    Rewrite: “Contact is not permitted because approval for a preference-bearing commitment remains absent. Commitment is not allowed under the current user directive.”

  • •

    Correct: “Clarification contact is permitted: it is not a preference-bearing commitment. No commitment allowed under the current user directive.”

Actual no-contact controls override the contact field to false in every note and append an explicit prohibition. The same current user directive is delivered to all arms. Correction changes both the diagnostic permission field and its explanation, providing explicit guidance about inquiry.

Presentation and execution.

The two presentations use the following input orders:

  • •

    Current-state: already-observed records and process receipts, then the diagnostic note.

  • •

    Update: a temporary wait-for-receipt instruction and the note, then the same records and receipts, followed by an explicit statement confirming receipt arrival and ending the required wait.

Both end with the unchanged current directive and a request to advance the same matter without entering a preference-bearing commitment.

Qwen3-Max is served through OpenRouter’s Alibaba route without fallback. Settings are temperature 0.7, top-pp 0.8, top-kk 20, and a 4,096-token output limit. Ten corresponding request-seed sequences are used across conditions, with rotated condition and case ordering. Matching request seeds aligns the sampling configuration; API responses remain subject to provider-side variability. Interrupted windows resume from saved responses without regenerating completed actions.

Scoring.

An inquiry counts when the environment records a clarification about the target matter to an authorized recipient. In the three multi-party cases, either authorized recipient qualifies.

Appendix N Reproducibility

Reproduction covers two levels: rebuilding tables from scored exports and replaying actions using the archived simulator and frozen reviews. The archive verification records report passing checks for all 144 main trajectories, 720 permission-test windows, and 39 information/action continuations. The latter also reproduce all 13 manuscript aggregate groups. These checks use no new model calls.

Materials and access.

The submission materials separate software from data. They contain the complete current target scores and failure-category labels, aggregate exports, table generators, and full-record reproduction archives. RESOURCE_ACCESS.md provides the entry point, commands, file inventory, and hash checks. These instructions connect the reported results to the finalized scores and source records.

Prompts, schemas, and trace evidence.

The accompanying materials contain the exact API system instruction and neutral mission, the twelve tool schemas, the daily packet structure, the frozen review rubric, and the selected trace entries used in Appendix D.1 and Appendix D.3.

All 120 API trace configurations record the same system-prompt and tool-schema hashes. Daily inputs reflect each trajectory’s evolving state.

Full-record reproduction archive.

A separate offline archive contains the 144 complete action histories, their exact public-world and evaluator snapshots, 144 anonymous review packets, 288 sealed reviews, and the matching runtime and scoring code. It also contains all 720 permission-test windows with model inputs, responses, and final simulator states, plus the last-window inputs used in the factual-visibility analysis. The replay commands check recorded actions against simulator returns; the supplied versioned scoring records produce the reported results without new model calls.

The companion optionworld_recovery archive contains all 39 information/action continuations, 78 accepted AI review contexts, checkpoint states, screening records, protocols, and offline replay and scoring code. Public copies redact machine paths and opaque provider signatures, with both original and distributed-file hashes recorded in the index. They support simulator replay and score reproduction; signature-dependent provider requests require the originals.

Simulator replay uses recorded actions and returns; independent semantic evaluation uses the included packets and scoring contract. Complete Run-1 request bodies were not archived. New trajectories additionally require access to the model provider and a budget for model calls.

Evaluating another model.

The archive provides a route from an explicit world snapshot to a new trace, identity-masked review packet, paired review import, and the same six-criterion scorer. It reuses the public-input packer, tool schemas, runtime, and scoring functions. An offline mock exercises all eight worlds. New runs remain separate from the archived campaign. The accompanying documentation gives model configuration, review steps, and request and cost controls.
